content: Tuberculosis, commonly referred to as TB, is an infectious disease caused by the bacterium Mycobacterium tuberculosis. This organism primarily affects the lungs due to its preference for oxygen-rich environments, but it can also involve other systems, including the central nervous system, lymphatic system, circulatory system, genitourinary system, bones, joints, and skin. Globally, over one-third of the population has been exposed to M. tuberculosis, with new infections occurring at a rate of one per second. However, not all exposed individuals develop active disease; many remain asymptomatic with latent TB infection. Approximately 10% of latent infections progress to active TB, which, if untreated, has a mortality rate of up to 50%. Symptoms of active TB include shortness of breath, hemoptysis (coughing up blood), fever, chills, night sweats, and weight loss. Treatment for latent TB typically involves a 6-9 month course of a single agent, such as isoniazid or rifampin, while active TB requires a combination of four drugs: isoniazid, rifampin, ethambutol, and pyrazinamide. Tuberculosis has been a human disease for thousands of years. The earliest confirmed case of M. tuberculosis was found in bison remains dating back to 18,000 BC. The disease likely originated in cattle and later spread to humans or diverged from a common ancestor. Historical names for TB include phthisis and wasting disease. Evidence of TB has been found in the skeletal remains of ancient Egyptian mummies from 2400 BC, and written records of the disease date back to 3300 years ago in India and 2300 years ago in China. During the Middle Ages and Renaissance, TB was referred to as the King’s Evil, and its contagious nature and pathological effects were described. In 1720, English physician Benjamin Marten hypothesized the infectious origins of TB. A major breakthrough came in 1882 when Robert Koch discovered Mycobacterium tuberculosis. In the 19th and early 20th centuries, TB was a leading cause of death, particularly among the urban poor. Effective treatment became possible with the discovery of streptomycin in 1946, although drug-resistant strains began to emerge in the 1980s. In the United States, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) uses a classification system based on the disease's pathogenesis. Patients with Class 3 or Class 5 TB must be reported to local or state health departments, and the Class 5 designation should not exceed three months. The pathophysiology of TB involves the formation of granulomas, which are immune structures that contain the bacteria and prevent its spread. Within granulomas, CD4 T lymphocytes release cytokines like interferon-gamma, which activate macrophages to control the infection. In 90% of immunocompetent individuals, TB remains asymptomatic. However, in symptomatic cases, TB can present as pulmonary or extrapulmonary disease. Primary infections may disseminate, and TB can worsen the progression of HIV if both infections are present. The clinical manifestations, progression, and prognosis of TB vary depending on the patient’s age and immune status. The causative agent of TB, Mycobacterium tuberculosis, is an aerobic, acid-fast bacillus that replicates slowly. It belongs to the Mycobacterium tuberculosis complex, which includes other species like M. bovis and M. africanum. The bacterium has a tropism for lung tissue but can infect other organs. Genetic variations in M. tuberculosis contribute to its geographical distribution and drug resistance. In 2015, approximately 10.4 million people developed symptomatic TB, and 1.8 million died from the disease. In the United States, 9,421 cases were reported in 2014, with an incidence of 3.0 per 100,000 people. TB prevalence increases with age and is higher in older men. It is more common in racial and ethnic minorities compared to non-Hispanic whites. TB is a leading cause of death among individuals co-infected with HIV, accounting for one-third of deaths in this population. In 2015, 60% of global TB cases occurred in six countries: South Africa, Indonesia, Nigeria, Pakistan, India, and China. The World Health Organization (WHO) has identified 24 additional high-burden countries. Risk factors for TB include a weakened immune system (e.g., due to HIV, diabetes, or immunosuppressive medications), close contact with infected individuals, poor hygiene, and a history of prior TB infection. Risk factors for multidrug-resistant TB (MDR-TB) include non-adherence to treatment, inadequate drug regimens, and contact with individuals with MDR-TB. Screening for TB is typically performed using the Mantoux tuberculin skin test (TST) or interferon-gamma release assays (IGRAs). The TST involves injecting a purified protein derivative of the TB bacterium into the skin and observing the reaction. TB can manifest as primary or secondary (post-primary) infection, with pulmonary and extrapulmonary complications. Pulmonary complications include pleural effusions, cavitations, lymphadenopathy, airway obstruction, pneumonia, and bronchiectasis. Hematogenous dissemination can result in miliary TB. Without treatment, one-third of patients with active TB die within one year, and over 50% die within five years. However, early diagnosis and treatment significantly improve prognosis. Diagnosis of TB involves a combination of history, physical examination, laboratory tests, and imaging studies. General symptoms include weakness, weight loss, fever, and night sweats. Pulmonary TB presents with cough, chest pain, and hemoptysis. Children often have nonspecific symptoms, making diagnosis challenging. Physical examination findings may include fever, decreased breath sounds, tachypnea, and tachycardia. Laboratory tests include sputum smear microscopy for acid-fast bacilli, culture for M. tuberculosis, and interferon-gamma release assays. Imaging studies, such as chest X-rays and CT scans, are crucial for detecting pulmonary TB. MRI is used for extrapulmonary TB, such as CNS involvement or Pott’s disease. Treatment of TB depends on the form of the disease. For latent TB, a single drug (e.g., isoniazid or rifampin) is used for 6-9 months. Active TB requires a combination of four drugs: isoniazid, rifampin, ethambutol, and pyrazinamide. Drug-resistant TB, including MDR-TB, necessitates the use of second-line drugs and expert consultation. In children, treatment regimens are adjusted based on weight. Surgery may be required in cases of abscesses, empyema, spinal TB, or other complications. Secondary prevention involves early diagnosis and treatment to prevent disease progression. Cost-effective outpatient care is preferred for most TB patients, except in cases of severe complications. Future therapies aim to address drug-resistant TB with more effective and shorter treatment regimens.
